standard.title: Unknown values in equations
standard.description: Find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction, using the properties of numbers and operations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise addition and subtraction as inverse operations and find unknown values in basic number sentences (AC9M3A01). They have not yet applied equivalence reasoning to equations with unknowns on either side, or used properties such as commutativity across multi-addend equations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction by applying number properties and relational thinking, and explain whether equations are true.

nodes.label: Equation as balance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that an equation means both sides have the same value, using a balance model.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a balance scale or diagram to represent one equation; explain what the equals sign means in terms of balance.
nodes.typical_width: Represent a range of true and false equations using balance scales and informal units; explain why 7 + 8 = 6 + 9 is true and 5 + 4 = 10 is false using balance reasoning.
wider: Create families of equivalent addition sentences that have the same total, using balance reasoning to verify
Investigate whether equations with three addends can be balanced in different ways (e.g. 2+2+3 = 2+3+2 = 3+2+2)

response_modes.reason: The equals sign is commonly misread as 'the answer comes next' rather than as a relational symbol meaning balance. Exposure to equations with expressions on both sides (e.g. 6+8 = □+10) is the resolution — single-answer-format equations reinforce the misconception.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who read the equals sign as 'write the answer here' cannot engage with Node 4's relational thinking tasks — finding unknowns in equations of the form a + b = □ + c requires understanding equality as balance, not as a command to compute.
success_criteria: Students can explain that both sides of an equation must have the same value
Students can identify whether a given equation is true or false and justify using a balance model

nodes.label: Inverse relationship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to find an unknown in a number sentence.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve one unknown-addend problem (e.g. 27 + □ = 63) by applying subtraction as the inverse operation; explain the reasoning.
nodes.typical_width: Use part-part-whole diagrams and bar models to represent and solve unknown-addend and unknown-total problems; explicitly articulate the inverse relationship (e.g. □ = 63 − 27 because subtraction undoes addition); apply to two-digit and three-digit problems.
wider: Investigate how the same bar model can generate multiple related equations (a+b=c, c−a=b, c−b=a), building fluency with the full fact family
Solve multi-step problems where two unknowns are constrained by the same equation structure

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from repeated practice deriving related subtraction facts from addition facts and vice versa. The connection between the inverse operation and the unknown position needs to become automatic before applying it to larger numbers.

success_criteria: Students can write the related subtraction sentence to solve an unknown-addend equation
Students can use a part-part-whole diagram to represent an unknown-addend problem and identify which part is missing

nodes.label: Commutativity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use commutativity to reason about equivalent expressions and simplify calculation.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate with materials or a number line that 5+2 = 2+5; use commutativity to find an easier calculation order for one multi-addend sum.
nodes.typical_width: Use number lines and materials to demonstrate commutative property; apply to multi-addend expressions (2+2+3 = 3+2+2); use commutativity to identify efficient calculation orders.
wider: Investigate which operations are commutative and which are not — testing subtraction and discussing why a−b ≠ b−a in general
Explore how commutativity of addition can simplify mental computation by choosing an easier order (e.g. reordering addends to make tens)
success_criteria: Students can show using materials or a number line that the order of addends does not change the sum
Students can use commutativity to reorder a multi-addend sum into a more convenient calculation

nodes.label: Relational thinking — find unknowns in equivalent sentences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can find unknown values in equations where both sides contain expressions (e.g. 6 + 8 = □ + 10), using relational thinking.
nodes.minimum_width: Find the unknown in one equation of the form a + b = □ + c by reasoning about what value makes both sides equal; explain the reasoning.
nodes.typical_width: Use relational thinking, balance models and number lines to find unknowns in equivalent number sentences; explain whether equations involving addition and subtraction are true by reasoning about the common difference or equivalent sums; apply to two-digit examples (e.g. 27 − 14 = 17 − 4).
wider: Generate families of equivalent equations starting from a known sum (e.g. all the equations equivalent to □ + □ = 14) and explore what patterns emerge
Investigate number sentences where the unknown appears on the left side (□ − 6 = 9) and compare the reasoning required to when it appears on the right

response_modes.reason: Students who only practise equations with the unknown on the right (a + b = □) do not develop relational thinking. Equations with expressions on both sides (a + b = □ + c) are the breadth that forces the shift from procedural calculation to equivalence reasoning.

The step from 'calculate both sides' to 'use the structure of the equation to find the unknown without calculating' requires explicit scaffolding — e.g. 'what do I need □ to be so that this side matches that side?' Teachers invest in making this reasoning move visible.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Equivalent number sentences are pedagogically rich — they connect arithmetic to early algebraic thinking, support number sense development, and provide a foundation for Year 5–6 algebra. Students who engage widely here develop the relational view of equality that supports all later equation work.
success_criteria: Students can find the unknown in an equation where both sides contain an expression (e.g. 6 + 8 = □ + 10)
Students can explain whether a given equation is true or false using relational reasoning (e.g. describing common differences on a number line)
